findings.title: Equal-order crypto providers are no longer rejected
findings.body: detectProvider used to fail startup when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by order() descending and silently keeps the first winner, logging the rest only at debug. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so a deployment that accidentally has two of those modules (the case the old check existed for) now boots with whichever ServiceLoader returns first. A FIPS provider can be ignored in favor of the non-FIPS default, or the reverse, with no error. Tie on order should still be a hard failure; only a strictly lower order (the new authz-client provider at 100) should be ignored.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider
findings.body: getBouncyCastleProvider is documented and used as the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) JCA provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the JDK keystore provider (typically SUN), not BouncyCastle. WildFlyElytronProvider correctly returns null when BC is absent. When this provider is the one CryptoIntegration selects, callers that register or use getBouncyCastleProvider() will treat a non-BC provider as BouncyCastle and either register the wrong provider or invoke BC-only algorithms against it and fail. Return null if no BC provider is available.

findings.title: New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementors
findings.body: order() was added as an abstract method on the public CryptoProvider SPI with no default. Any out-of-tree or not-yet-updated CryptoProvider implementation no longer compiles or loads. A default such as order() returning 0 would keep old providers working and still let the in-tree providers (200) and AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100) win via the new sort.

findings.title: ECDSA tests use one P-256 key and only check a symmetric round trip
findings.body: The suite generates a single KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") key (platform default, P-256) and reuses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. R and S are therefore always ~32-byte P-256 integers, then padded to 48 or 66 bytes. The only assertion is that asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(rs)) equals rs. A conversion that drops high bytes, mishandles the DER sign byte, or emits unverifiable ASN.1 still passes, and ES384/ES512 are never exercised at their real coordinate sizes. Generate a key on the matching curve (P-256/P-384/P-521) and check Signature.verify on the DER form produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER.
